en: The Eastern Sea If-Exposition (Donghai jiejie) Composed by Liuzi Thou of the Tang Dynasty Interpreted by the Qing Dynasty Monk Shixian [Note: The title *Donghai jiejie* is traditionally attributed to Liang Su of the Tang dynasty;
this specific colophon identifies the author as Liuzi Thou and the commentator as the Qing monk Shixian.]
Regarding the "Sea of the East": Long ago, there was the renowned Confucian scholar of the Tang dynasty, Liu Zihou. He took pity on those who study Buddhism, whose views and understandings differ;
regarding the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, their faith and slander are not uniform. The stakes involved therein are as vast as the difference between heaven and abyss.
Desiring to enable them to know what to adopt and what to reject, so that they may reach the ultimate realization of the nature and mind, he composed this essay. First:
Those who study Confucianism have already set aside Buddhist principles without further investigation; those who study Buddhism, moreover, treat the written texts with careless indifference.
Among the few intelligent individuals there may be, most lack the faculty of faith; even if they possess the faculty of faith, [they remain deficient].
Furthermore, there is a lack of wisdom, which causes profound texts and abstruse meanings to remain hidden within fragmented manuscripts and scattered fragments, with no one able to penetrate them.

Is this not to be lamented? Therefore, I have clarified their significance to compose this commentary, hoping it may serve as a small aid for encouraging and inspiring those at the beginning stage of practice.
When Donghaier traveled overland and ascended the heights of Mengzhu, he found two gourds. He hollowed them out and polished their outer shells to play with them.
He filled them with seawater mixed with excrement, soil, and parasitic worms until the stench was unbearable.
He sealed them with dense stones, lifted them up, and cast them into the sea. After some time had passed, he went by that spot and said, "Was this merely discarded filth?"

"Donghaeryak" (Eastern Sea-If) refers to the name of a sea deity, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) Yuhongfa. This is because the sea deity presides over the ocean, just as the Great Being presides over the Dharma;

thus, he is compared to this deity. "Traveling by land" means leaving the ocean of the Pure Land to reach the shore of the Sahā world, just as the sea deity leaves the ocean to travel upon land. "Mengzhu" is the name of a place; Qufu calls it A. It is high.

Descending upon uneven ground serves as a metaphor for the perilous path of the triple world (*tridhātu*). This means that having personally emerged from birth and death, one enters the triple world again to deliver sentient beings suffering in *duḥkha*;
hence it is said, "ascending the heights of Mengzhu. Second, the two gourds serve as metaphors for the two types of faculties: those of faith and those of slander.
The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings are called "gourds. Because causes and conditions have converged, they are said to "obtain" them; thus, one hollows them out.
"Shaking its horn to play" refers to the Great Being’s playful exercise of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*), which does not grasp at the marks of sentient beings.
"Hollowing out" (*kū*) means emptiness; "shaking off" (*zhen*) means to remove; "horn" (*xi*) means the child.

This speaks of emptying away the child and using a gourd as a plaything, which precisely illustrates being free from the marks of sentient beings while taking the salvation of beings as one's play. "Taking the water of the ocean" refers to preaching the Dharma.
As for "mixed with manure and soil": when sentient beings hear the Dharma, their wisdom is mixed with ignorance. "Manure and soil" is a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*);

"earthworms" is a metaphor for birth and death (*saṃsāra*). The causes and effects of afflictions do not go beyond the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), and the various types of birth and death are likewise contained therein.

"Not departing from the twelve" refers to the "stench," which is like suffering. The afflictions of birth and death are so difficult to endure that they are called a "stench" that cannot be confronted.

"Mist" and "stone" are metaphors for fundamental ignorance; because one fails to realize it for even a single thought-moment, it is called an "obstruction. "Casting into the sea" [refers to the ultimate transcendence].

This is illustrated by the analogy of entering birth and death. Although sentient beings of the past may have heard the Dharma and planted small roots of goodness, they remain long in birth and death, unable to attain liberation, because they are shrouded by ignorance.
Even when they encounter spiritual friends who offer exhortation and guidance, their faculties differ in being mature or immature;
thus, there are those for whom the aspiration arises and those for whom it does not. Those in whom it arises follow the teachings and practice; those in whom it does not...

Because they violate the teachings while clinging to their own principles, two gourds are taken as a metaphor. However, when a Great Being delivers sentient beings, it is like parents instructing their children:
they do not provide special instruction only to the filial child, nor do they abandon the rebellious child.

Therefore, even if one does not believe, the Bodhisattva still preaches the Dharma for them. Furthermore, he constantly observes their spiritual capacity to bring it forth; and even after time has passed—
"To have passed beyond" refers to waiting for the opportune moment. Having undergone the cycle of transmigration for a long time, it is called "exceeding the time.
Because past affinities have been mutually established, it is termed "passing. To say, "Is this why you discard the refuse? is a phrase intended to awaken him. It means:
"Did you not plant roots of goodness in the past? Are you still casting aside birth and death now? The intention is to cause him to resolve his mind [upon enlightenment].
Because he was mindful of the Buddha, he questioned him.
One of them called out at the top of his voice, saying, "I am the Great Ocean!

This is a metaphor for those who violate the teachings while clinging to abstract principles; calling out at the top of one's voice represents the state of being startled, suspicious, and unable to believe.
"I am the great ocean," he said, speaking thus to dismiss the facts in favor of abstract principle.
Donghaeryak laughed heartily and said, "How strange! Now, as for this great ocean: to its east there is no east;
to its west there is no west; to its north there is no north; and to its south there is no south. At dawn it bathes the sun and brings it forth; at night it washes over the constellations."
The Star: It contains the sun and raises the light of the jewel-fire of the yin to serve as its illumination.
Dust and mist do not dwell within it; they must be swept away to the western marshes. Therefore, in its vastness, its depth, its purity, and its radiance, nothing can compare to it.

This metaphor describes how the Great Being (Mahāsattva) expounds the ocean of the Buddha’s true nature (*dharmatā*) to reveal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). "Ya! is an expression of opening one's mouth;
it signifies astonishment. "Is this not strange? is a form of reproof. From "Now, as for... onwards, the correct principle is fully demonstrated. Indeed, the ocean of nature is boundless.

Therefore, there is no distinction of east, west, south, or north. The luminosity of the ocean of nature externally encompasses the sun, moon, and stars, while internally it contains all manner of jewels.
This external encompassing is spiritual power (*ṛddhi*); this internal containment is wisdom (*prajñā*). This is what is meant by the complete perfection of all virtues.

Furthermore, the sun is a metaphor for the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), while the stars and moon are metaphors for the various *nirmāṇakāyas* (emanation bodies) that appear according to the capacities of beings.

The appearance of the *saṃbhogakāya* in the world is called "dawn," and its *parinirvāṇa* is called "night. Although the traces of the *saṃbhogakāya* undergo birth and extinction, the essence of the Dharma is eternally serene. When the spiritual faculties of sentient beings have matured...

He then manifests the Buddha-body to deliver and liberate them; when his conditions are exhausted, he enters extinction, whereupon he again manifests transformation-bodies according to the various types of beings to guide them.
Although these various manifestations appear, they all collectively do not transcend the ocean of nature (*xinghai*);

this is what is meant by "encompassing from without. The fire within the *skandhas* is a metaphor for supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); the jewels are metaphors for meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). All three arise fully from the nature; this is...
Internally complete. Because the ocean of nature is pure, the dust and mist do not abide. "Dust and mist" refers to the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling;
this means that all evils have been utterly exhausted. The "Great Yin" is the moon; within the great ocean, the fire-light constantly arises.
This is called the "fire of the aggregates" (*skandha-agni*). *Shi* means the edge of water; it signifies that the great ocean does not coexist with dust and mist, but must carry them to its shores.
Likewise, the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom does not dwell together with afflictions (*kleśa*), but must sever them until they are completely exhausted before it ceases.
The four characters "profound," "vast," "luminous," and "pure" summarize the preceding text. Being without the four directions constitutes "profundity."
"O Deva! This light externally encompasses and internally possesses all things. To be free from dust is purity. 'There is none like me' is a term of praise;
it means that with the exception of the Buddha, all others have not yet attained this profound and vast utility of luminous purity.
Even if they possess it, it is merely partial and not ultimate."
Now you are but a discarded drop from the ocean, sharing the same substance as dung and soil. You dwell among the stinking and decayed, living with parasites and worms;
your space is but a span wide, and yet it is so dark and obscure. To equate yourself with the ocean—is this not shameful and pitiable?
Do you desire it? I shall pry open the rock for you, break the gourd, and wash away the mass of filth into the Great [Ocean].
"Is it possible for a child to remain on a desolate island as previously described?
This metaphor refutes biased views and demonstrates the path of correct practice. Now, regarding sentient beings and Buddhas..."
Although they share the same mind, sentient beings are deluded and inverted; they abandon the ocean to recognize a bubble, pointing to the bubble as the ocean.
Upon hearing of the true ocean, they instead reject it as false. Such individuals are truly to be pitied.
Now, those who cling to emptiness calculate that the deluded mind within the square inch of the five aggregates is their original face, and claim it is no different from the Buddha’s.
Second: It is like regarding the foul water in a gourd as being the great ocean; it would be no different from the actual sea.

One does not realize that the substance of the mind is vast and expansive, encompassing the empty worlds of the ten directions, such that sentient beings and all Buddhas are gathered within a single thought-moment, rather than being confined within the space of a square inch.
This is just as the great ocean is not confined within a gourd. Upon hearing the teaching of the Western Pure Land, Maitreya...

Regarding the ocean-nature of the Dharma, they calculate it to be outside of the mind and thus give rise to doubt and slander; it is like hearing of the true ocean and yet regarding it as non-existent.
Although Amitābha does not abandon sentient beings, sentient beings themselves reject him. It is like the great ocean, which does not refuse a single drop.
A single drop cast aside from the great ocean; hence it is called "the ocean’s discarded drop. The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings have afflictions as their substance;
therefore, it is said they are of the same essence as excrement and soil. "Foul" refers to suffering (*duḥkha*); "decayed" refers to impermanence (*anitya*).
"Cáo" (曹) means "companion" or "partner. This body is a companion to the multitude of impermanent things; it is not real. *Jiāo* (蟯) and *yóu* (蠱) [parasites] within the body...
It is a worm; it serves as a metaphor for the twelve classes of beings. What is called "this body" is a place where these twelve classes cohabit;
it is not liberation. It is but a mere six-foot frame, hence the term *zhǐ* (a cubit). It is shrouded in ignorance and devoid of wisdom, hence the term "darkness.
To grasp this square-inch deluded mind and this six-foot deluded body, claiming them to be identical to the wondrous functioning of the Buddha—is this not perversion? Therefore, he rebukes it.

He said, "It is shameful and pitiable. He asked: "The Sūtra says, 'The liberation of all Buddhas should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings,' and it also says, 'Contemplate the true reality of the body;
contemplate the Buddha in the same way. Is it not the case that the bodies and minds of sentient beings are no different from those of the Buddhas?
Yet you wish to distinguish between delusion and awakening, and to discourse on the holy and the ordinary. Is this not like being blind and yet claiming to see space?"
"Is it a flower? He replied, "As stated in the sutras: this is precisely observing the true within the false, without clinging to the false as being true.
It is like taking a single drop to observe the ocean, without clinging to that drop as being the ocean.

Furthermore, as for a single drop of water and the water of the great ocean, how do their moist nature differ? Yet, once separated from the great ocean and mixed with filth and soil, how could it [be the same]?"
To say that [the drop] is itself the ocean is to falsely perceive the true as being the conventional; yet one should not cling to this view. The mind is also like this.
Therefore, know that while the nature of water has no distinction, it is permissible to seek the plan of returning to the ocean.

However, it is not permissible to fixate upon a single drop and claim it to be the great ocean. Please consider this for a moment. The passage beginning with "If you desire this... is abbreviated below.
He demonstrates the benefits of practice to encourage them. When he says, "I shall act for you," it does not mean that he is performing that practice on their behalf;

rather, it refers to attributing the merit of transformation to himself so that its benefits reach others. "Picking out stones" is a metaphor for severing fundamental ignorance (*avidyā*). "Breaking the gourd" is a metaphor for escaping the triple world (*traidhātuka*).
"Washing away filth" is a metaphor for departing from the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*). "The great wilderness" is a metaphor for the *dharmadhātu* of tranquil light (*śāntaprabhā*).
The realm is vast and boundless; the "island" is a metaphor for the Land of Ultimate Bliss, rising high above the ten directions.

What has been described above is the profound, great, luminous, and pure function of all Buddhas. To know that others do not believe it, yet to continue preaching the Dharma for them out of necessity, is because the Great Being’s compassionate heart is too intense;
though there may be no benefit in the present, it serves as a cause for their deliverance in the future.
"It is but a matter of conditions.
The man in the cesspool remained unperturbed and did not say, "I am indeed the same as you. What more do I seek from you? My nature is simply this:
that which is foul remains foul of itself; it is insufficient to harm my purity. That which is narrow remains narrow of itself..."
The narrow cannot harm my breadth; the obscure is naturally obscure and cannot harm my clarity. Furthermore, filth is also the ocean;
the narrow and the obscure are also the ocean. Sudden departures and effortless arrivals—who among them is not the ocean?
You may go; do not disturb me.

This metaphor illustrates how one hears the teaching but does not believe it, using mere words to reject it. An ordinary person of the mundane world, though possessing some small wisdom, does not sever the afflictions;
therefore, they are likened to "filth-water. Because such a person hears the teaching but does not believe it, it is said that [the Buddha] does not speak to them.

"I am certainly the same" is a statement based on principle. When discussing the essence of principle, there is no duality between the living being and the Buddha; hence, it is said, "I am certainly the same. I...
Furthermore, what more could be sought from you? These words of self-sufficiency are precisely what was set forth in the preceding text: the realm of all Buddhas.
This is because one manifests innate nature (*xingde*) through cultivated virtue (*xiude*). Now, those who cling to principle have a mistaken understanding;
they speak only of innate nature while abandoning cultivated virtue. Therefore it is said: "My nature is also just like this. This refers to my mind.

It also possesses profound, vast, and luminous utility, lacking nothing whatsoever. One does not realize that speaking of food while painting cakes provides no benefit to a hungry stomach and merely exhausts body and speech.
The following section will specifically set forth the views of partial emptiness; therein, filth shall not impair purity.
To say that the essence of nature is pure means it is not defiled by birth and death. To say it is narrow does not exclude its vastness;
this means the essence of nature is expansive and is not confined by physical forms or vessels. To say it is obscure does not exclude its luminosity;

this refers to the essence of nature being radiant and not shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*). "Filth, narrowness, and obscurity" refer to the entire reality of the ocean of phenomena, which is non-dual and without distinction.
"Distinct. Therefore, it says "also. "Tu-ran" describes the manner of coming and going; it serves as a metaphor for appearing and disappearing within birth and death.
Since all these are the wondrous principle of the original nature, it asks, "Who is not the ocean? Question: As you have described above, there has never been anything that is not so.
Why do you criticize me so severely? Answer: It is indeed as you ask. Although your words are correct, your intent—
That is not so. For instance, regarding the "Three Non-harmings," such expressions also appear within Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras.

Nevertheless, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have never dismissed the practice of cultivation to speak of the principle-nature alone. Now, deluded people cling to a fixed, defiled, narrow, and obscure state, yet claim for themselves purity and vastness;
they do not realize that when afflictions manifest before them, their very "purity" becomes a source of harm. This is the measure.

To allow nothing to enter is a source of harm; this is made clear by the pervasiveness of such afflictions. To invert right and wrong is a source of harm; this is made clear by the present state of affairs.
Even the single thought-moment of the present cannot guarantee freedom from harm, let alone the future cycle of birth and death—how could one know for oneself?
Though it is said that there is no harm, this is precisely what constitutes a great harm. It is like when the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas occasionally manifest to transform and deliver sentient beings.
Manifesting afflictions while the mind remains free of discrimination—this is truly the impure not harming the pure.

Whether cut by a blade or anointed with fragrance, remaining equal and without hatred or love; showing universal compassion equally toward Rāhula and Devadatta—this is truly the narrow not harming the broad.
Practicing what is not the Path while attaining mastery of the Buddha-Path—this is truly the obscure not harming the luminous. And now...
"To take the limited wisdom of an ordinary person and equate it with the Buddha-wisdom is to incur one's own fault; is this not the height of error?
You may go; do not disturb me. These were words of refusal, uttered by a man of the Chan school who was rigidly attached to his principles.
Upon first hearing the teachings and principles, his mind was immediately and greatly offended; thus he spoke as he did.
When he heard Ruoy’s words, he wailed and prayed, saying: "I have been poisoned by this for a long time.
I considered it to be naturally so and not something to be questioned. Now you tell me of the vastness of the ocean, and yet you address me as one who has abandoned the old ocean."
It is dung. I am becoming increasingly desperate. To surge my *Shu* River is insufficient to clear its blockage; to swirl my waves is insufficient to bore through the belly of this gourd.
Even if one were able to do so, it would take years and months to reach the end. I pray that you will deign to have pity on me.
This metaphor refers to a practitioner who follows the teachings. Upon first hearing the Buddha-dharma, they give rise to great repentance and realization, vowing their hearts upon liberation;
thus, they weep and offer prayers. "I have been poisoned for a long time. Here, "poison" (dú) means harm.
The afflictions (*kleśa*) of birth and death destroy my Dharma-body and extinguish my life of wisdom; hence they are called poison. Having remained submerged for many kalpas, it is therefore said:
"It has been long. Furthermore, "long" refers to having constantly harbored a mind weary of suffering, yet not yet finding the path to liberation;
it means that one's roots of goodness are about to ripen and the spiritual capacity is on the verge of being activated. This is indeed so. Regarding the aspect of "reality":
prior to hearing the teaching, one thought that the afflictions of birth and death were truly immutable and that weariness with them was useless. Now, having heard...
The ocean of the Buddha’s merit is vast and immeasurable; thus one knows that birth can lead to Buddhahood. Therefore it is said: "He informs me of the greatness of the ocean.
Furthermore, one knows that in former lives one has sown seeds and established a karmic connection with the Buddha, yet I myself have been deluded and turned my back upon him.
One abandons birth and death; hence it is said: "I cast away the excrement of the old ocean with my eyes. This is the path for transcendence and the method for liberation.
Seeking it and wearying of it must become increasingly urgent; thus it is said: "It becomes more pressing. The following passages all consist of words concerning knowing one's own capacity.
"Surging and flooding" is a metaphor for the discrimination of limited wisdom. "Opening the blockage" is a metaphor for destroying ignorance. "Whirling..."
The "wave" is a metaphor for the movement of subtle merit. The "hollow belly" is a metaphor for exiting the three realms; that one is able to do so is a figurative expression.
"Exhausting months and years" refers to the protracted passage of vast kalpas. "Fortunately, have pity on me" is a plea for the Buddha’s compassionate acceptance.
The Dragon King of the Eastern Sea then tore open rocks and smashed gourds, casting them onto the plains of Mengzhu;
he swept away their filth upon the islands of the Great Wilderness, and the waters returned to the sea, so that everything previously described was fully recovered.

This metaphor illustrates the benefit of practicing in accordance with the teachings. Ignorance is suddenly shattered, like piercing a stone; birth and death are forever extinguished, like breaking a gourd.
One takes one’s final leave of the three realms, hence it is said: "He casts himself into Mengzhu. The nine lotuses are personally reached, hence it is said:
"The island of Great Wilderness. By means of the ordinary mind, the Buddha-mind is perceived, hence it is said: "The water returns to the sea."
Yet that former one ultimately remains amidst the foul and corrupt without changing.
This is a metaphor for the harm of violating the teachings while clinging to emptiness; it is like the water held in the gourd being no different from that of the great ocean.

They do not realize that the stone has not yet been removed and the impurity has not yet been cleared away; nor have the waters returned to the sea. Although water is non-dual, it differs in its breadth or narrowness and its purity or impurity.
Furthermore, they cling to the notion that both the impure and the narrow are already the sea, failing to realize that they will ultimately rot and decay without being able to undergo transformation.
Is this not tragic? Now, those who cling to their own principles claim, "My mind is the Buddha; what need is there for..."
To see Amitābha again is to realize that the mind itself is the Pure Land; why then must one necessarily be reborn in Sukhāvatī?

One does not realize that the phenomena of karma within ignorance and the cycle of birth and death are fiercely blazing. Although the wondrous mind exists, it has not yet been personally realized, nor has the great function of the Buddha been attained.
Furthermore, you cling to the notion that the afflictions of birth and death are all themselves bodhi and nirvana; who then would not be the Buddha-dharma?
Yet, unaware that birth and death manifest before you, you remain as before in a state of bewildered uncertainty—where could there possibly be nirvana? Ignorance arises in a flash.
Yet they continue to invert right and wrong; who, then, is the awakened one of Bodhi? Their lifelong idle talk leads to long kalpas of sinking and delusion—how can one not feel heartache for this?

Now there are two who claim to be Buddhas. Both have emerged from the ocean of Vairocana, yet they weep amidst the filth of the five turbidities, are confined within the gourd of the three realms of existence, are obstructed by the stone of ignorance, and are mixed with the parasites of the twelve classes of beings.
When someone questions them, one of them says: "I am the Buddha, Vairocana."
The five turbidities, the three realms of existence, and the twelve categories of ignorance are all empty. All things are neither good nor evil; there is no cause and no effect;
there is no cultivation and no realization; there is no Buddha and no sentient beings—all are non-existent. What, then, is there for me to seek?
This synthesizes the preceding metaphors. Although both are students of the Buddha, their knowledge and views differ; thus, it is said that both are "Buddhas.
These two individuals represent the two types of spiritual capacities: those who have faith and those who harbor slander. Vairocana means "Pervading All Places."
This is the Buddha’s Dharma-body, also named the Ocean of the Nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This Dharma-body is of one essence with all Buddhas and sentient beings;
therefore, it is said they emerge together. As for the five turbidities (*pañca-kāṣāya*): first, the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kāṣāya*), up to the fifth, the turbidity of life (*āyuṣ-kāṣāya*).

These five all take defilement as their defining characteristic; thus, they are metaphorically compared to excrement. The "three existences" (*tri-bhava*) refers to the three realms—namely, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)—which are separated [from one another].
Because they undergo different experiences, they are called "realms" (*dhātu*). Because cause and effect are not non-existent, they are termed "existence" (*bhava*).
The three existences confine and limit sentient beings; thus, they are likened to a gourd. The four great elements confine and limit the six consciousnesses, and the principle is likewise;

thus, they are all so named. Ignorance obstructs and impedes the *dharmatā*; thus, it is likened to a stone. The twelve categories of beings do not depart from the three realms, just like the *rāji* and *krimi* worms.
He does not leave the human belly. When someone questions him, that person is precisely a Great Being of the Four Reliances. One person is one who violates the teachings and clings to emptiness;
this refers to "I," the Buddha. This corresponds to the aforementioned "I am the great ocean. That "all is empty" is precisely what he clings to.
The emptiness of the five turbidities corresponds to the aforementioned: "filth is insufficient to harm purity. The emptiness of the three realms corresponds to the aforementioned: "narrowness."
This is insufficient to harm Guang. The twelve categories of ignorance are all empty; when combined with the profound darkness above, they are insufficient to harm the light.
Goodness pertains to humans and devas; evil pertains to the three paths. Cause and effect, cultivation, and realization are common to the four types of noble beings.
Regarding those who cling to emptiness, there are two kinds: first, those whose minds achieve spontaneous understanding; second, those who hear it explained by others. As for the mind...
"One who seeks liberation on their own finds it difficult to cure their illness; one who hears from another may later be healed.
The questioner said, "What you have spoken of is 'nature' (xing). There is also 'phenomenon' (shi). Now, nature and phenomenon are two yet one, and one yet two.
If one holds fast to the one and remains fixed therein, then great calamity will arrive. The man said, "Go, sir!"

"Do not disturb me. This indicates correct understanding so that one may recognize faults and afflictions. It is said that "nature" has three meanings: the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the meaning of the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the meaning of the middle (*madhyama*).
As previously explained, [some] attain only the meaning of emptiness but do not understand the middle and the provisional; furthermore, there is emptiness and existence...

The three kinds refer to biased emptiness (*piān kōng*), cessation emptiness (*duàn kōng*), and true emptiness (*zhēn kōng*). The preceding discussion concerned only biased emptiness and cessation emptiness;
one has not yet attained the principle of true emptiness, so how could such a person know the nature? If one awakens to true emptiness, one will naturally not negate the myriad dharmas.
Therefore, it is known that [the previous view] was not understood. The passage beginning with "There is something to be done" is precisely the remedy for this ailment.
The words regarding the administration of medicine: "Nature" is identical to "Principle. This means that Principle and Phenomena are one yet eternally two, and two yet eternally one.
When they are perfectly interfused, great efficacy is established; when one clings to the one, great affliction arises. Success or failure rests with the person.
This has nothing to do with the Buddha-dharma. Question: What is meant by "one yet two" and "two yet one"? Answer: As the Patriarch said:
"Cultivation and realization are not non-existent; defilement is simply not permitted. These words are precisely it. Now, as for "cultivation and realization are not non-existent":

This is the principle of phenomena (*dharma*). "Defiled" is not permitted; this is the principle of reality (*tattva*). These two phrases of meaning and principle are mutually inclusive and mutually interfused;
neither may be discarded unilaterally. Because the upper phrase contains the meaning of the lower, one speaks of cultivation and realization despite the absence of cultivation and realization.

Because the lower phrase contains the meaning of the upper, one speaks of defilement and purity despite the absence of defilement and purity. This is the purport of the non-duality of phenomena and principle. If [one were to speak] solely...
To cling to the existence of cultivation and realization is identical to the provisional teachings of the Two Vehicles.

To single-mindedly cling to being unstained is identical to the Naturalists (Svabhāvavādins) and likewise to the provisional teachings; in the former case, one merely prizes meritorious achievement, which is a shallow error.
In the latter case, one negates cause and effect, which is a profound harm. Therefore it is said that the great affliction has arrived. In the present life, one loses [the Way].
The benefits of diligent cultivation will, in the future, instead bring about the calamity of downfall; how can one not fear this?

Furthermore, regarding the words and phrases of the Patriarchs, there are those where "the words are partial but the meaning is perfect. Often, those of meager intelligence produce interpretations based merely on the literal phrasing, causing the *amṛta* (nectar) to instead become a poisonous drug—this is truly lamentable. Question: What is meant by "words are partial but the meaning is perfect"?
[The Master] Yuan replied: "As Master Zhigong said: 'The five desires, greed, and anger are the Buddha; hell is itself heaven. The wise know that the mind is the Buddha;
the ignorant delight in going to the West. This is what is meant by 'the words are biased, but the meaning is complete. Now I shall explain this:
it means that if a person can contemplate the objects of the five desires, as well as greed, anger, and delusion, [as they truly are]..."
Like flowers in the sky, they do not give rise to discrimination; one should know that such a person is called a Buddha.

Therefore it is said that the greed, anger, and delusion of the five desires are the Buddha. Furthermore, one contemplates the appearances of suffering and joy in the hells and heavens as being like events in a dream;
thus, one does not give rise to attachment toward heaven, nor does one give rise to fear toward hell. Both are equal.
Therefore it is said: "Hell is itself heaven. The wise know that the mind is Buddha; the ignorant delight in going to the West.
These two lines emphasize the two characters "knowing the mind. This means that if one knows the mind is Buddha, this person’s recitation of the Buddha's name is that of a wise person.
If one does not know this, then even though they delight in going to the West, they remain an ignorant person. Thus says the wise one.
What [the text] refers to as "upper-upper grade" is what the foolish call "lower-lower grade. These two terms are fundamentally not in contradiction with the essential principle of the Pure Land.
Yet, those who hold erroneous views cling to this and claim that *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) is the practice of the foolish.
How could it be that only the lower-lower grade exists in the Western Paradise, while the upper-upper grade does not? Furthermore, the "lower grades" refer to those here [in this world].
Even though one may be a fool, if they are born in the Pure Land, they will enter the stage of non-retrogression and can no longer be called a fool.
Not recognizing one's own folly, yet instead claiming others to be fools—how can this be called wisdom? Therefore, what is valued is grasping the essential meaning.
One must be cautious regarding the handling of the text; let me provide one example to illustrate this, for upon reflection it will become clear.
One person said: "Alas! I have been poisoned for a long time. I have exhausted my strength, yet it has not sufficed to remove ignorance;
I have exhausted my wisdom, yet it has not sufficed to transcend the three realms of existence or leave behind the five turbidities—how different I am from those of the twelve categories of beings!"
Furthermore, as for the duration of these great and small kalpas, it is impossible to know. What can be done?
This clarifies that practitioners who follow the teachings, recognizing their own lack of power, speak these words of self-examination.

As we are currently in the age of the Dharma’s decline (*mofa*), human faculties have become increasingly dull and their dispositions increasingly coarse. Generally speaking, there are two types of people, namely:
First, the ignorant; second, the mad. As for the ignorant, who are utterly bewildered and lack understanding, there is truly no need to discuss them.

As for the mad, their deluded minds aspire to the lofty and sublime, constantly wishing to leap over stages. They regard this Dharma-door of Buddha-remembrance as nothing more than weeds and refuse, even feeling contempt and shame toward it;
how much less would they be willing to practice it? This is due to nothing other than their lack of self-knowledge. An ancient said: "To know others requires wisdom."

Self-knowledge leads to clarity; indeed, in this present age, those who possess self-knowledge are already rare. The analogies combined within the text can each be understood accordingly. Regarding the mention of *kalpas*:
one small *kalpa* consists of one cycle of increase and decrease in human lifespan.

Accumulating these small *kalpas* until eighty such cycles have passed constitutes one great *kalpa*. Furthermore, by accumulating these great and small *kalpas*, [one reaches the full duration of a world-system].
When it reaches a point where it can no longer be numbered, it is called one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*. What is termed "unknowable" is precisely that which cannot be numbered.
According to the teachings of the Tripitaka, a Bodhisattva must undergo cultivation for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before finally attaining Buddhahood;
yet, those who regress are many, while those who advance are few. This clarifies the difficulty of achieving success through one's own power alone. Indeed, this applies to all dharma-gates.

All [paths] that rely on one’s own power to emerge from birth and death are difficult; only the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha relies both upon one’s own power and the power of others, and is therefore easy.

Because it is easy, it can be accomplished in a single lifetime; because they are difficult, they remain unfulfilled throughout vast eons. The point of benefit or harm, gain or loss, lies precisely here.
Thus, by knowing what is difficult and what is easy, one knows benefit and harm; by knowing benefit and harm, one knows what to reject and what to adopt. Otherwise—
Many have lost their footing on the path ahead; many have taken the wrong road.

While in an age of true dharma, there may still be those who can achieve birth and death through their own power, such people are rarely heard of in this age of the final dharma. Since one is now unable to rely on one's own power, one seeks the power of another;
therefore, I ask: what should be done?
The questioner then recounted the matters of the Western Land and was instructed to cultivate the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection.

This discourse on the non-duality of emptiness and existence moved the Sage, who took pity upon him, received him, and led him to the realm of Ultimate Bliss, whereby he was able to cast off all manner of evils.
Having accumulated the myriad practices and dwelling on the ground of the sages, one attains the same knowledge and vision as the Buddha.
This clarifies the benefits of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). The Sanskrit term *samādhi* is translated here as "right reception" (*zhèngshòu*).

This means that when right mindfulness is present before one, one does not undergo any [defiled] sensations. One who attains this *samādhi* will certainly see the Buddha in the present or in the future.
Regarding "one emptiness and existence": this refers to being mindful without mindfulness, and arising without arising. Question: If it is empty, not a single dharma can be established;
if it is existent, the myriad dharmas are in disarray. These two are contradictory; how can they be called "one"? Answer:
Formerly, when Chan Master Tianyi Huai revealed the Pure Land teachings, he said: "If one is born, one is certainly born; if one departs, one truly departs."
"It does not go. This is the principle of the identity of emptiness and existence. Now, to be born is to be definitively born;
this is existence (*yu*). To go is in truth not to go; this is emptiness (*kong*). Although there are two words, their meaning has never been two. The Master further said:
"It is like a wild goose passing through the vast sky, its reflection sinking into the cold water. The goose leaves no trace of its path, and the water has no reflection to retain."
"Mind. This is a self-explanation of the preceding passage. Please understand that through this analogy, the intended meaning will become clear by itself.

Now, the practitioner's five aggregates (skandhas) are called "geese. The mind of mindfulness directed toward the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti), which is present before one, is fundamentally vertical and pervasive;
therefore, it is likened to the vast sky. A single lifetime of the body does not endure long before it perishes; therefore, it is termed...
It is like a goose passing through the sky. Although the physical form of the illusion undergoes arising and ceasing, the nature of mindfulness is fundamentally without arising or ceasing;

hence it is called "a goose passing through the vast sky. The Pure Land is free from all feverish afflictions, hence it is called "cold water. Here in this world one recites the Buddha's name, while in that land the flowers bloom.
As soon as diligence and indolence are distinguished, prosperity and decay suddenly diverge; hence it is said, "the shadow sinks. Furthermore, in this land...

The cessation of the shadows here is called "the geese passing"; the arising of the shadows there is called "the reflections sinking. This ceasing and that arising occur simultaneously, without any sequence; therefore, they may be used as a metaphor.
These two lines explain the aforementioned "arising" as being definitively arising. The phrase regarding the geese signifies the absence of any trace left behind;

this clarifies that sentient beings do not go [to another realm]. The phrase regarding the water signifies the absence of any intention to retain a reflection; this clarifies the [nature of] all phenomena.
The Buddha does not come. Why? If there were one who goes, there must be a path; if there is a path, there must be time.
How then could there be cessation here and birth there in a manner that leaves no interval between them? If there were one who comes, there would be footprints;
if there are footprints, then this exists while that is absent, and thus he could not be omnipresent. How then could he manifest his response throughout the ten directions?
The simultaneous reception and guidance [of beings] should be understood as the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) being thus:
neither existent nor non-existent. How could one possibly entertain conceptual thought regarding this? These two phrases explain the preceding statement that "in reality, there is no going.

While the teaching on phenomena clarifies only the absence of going, the analogy additionally manifests the absence of coming; this is merely a secondary explanation. Question: Since it is said that sentient beings do not go, [how can they be received?]
Furthermore, it is said that if the Buddhas do not come, then those born in the Western Paradise must either remain right here, or else have no specific location at all.
Is this not like something seen in a dream—something that is not real? Answer: Have you not considered the phrase "the shadow sinks into the cold water"?
To say the shadow sinks into the cold water reveals that there is indeed a real transformation-birth (upapāduka) in the West.
As for this body, since its characteristics of coming and going are fundamentally unattainable, it is said that it neither goes nor comes.
Why are you so deeply bewildered and distressed? To eliminate all evils is the virtue of severance (*prahāṇa*); to accumulate the myriad practices is the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna*);
to dwell in the holy stages is the true cause consisting of the forty-one positions; and to share the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is what is meant by "opening, showing, awakening, and entering."
Regarding the principle of entering [the Way]:
that person mentioned previously ultimately remains identical to the twelve classes of beings and does not change.
This clarifies the harm of not reciting the Buddha’s name. As for the "twelve classes," they refer to those born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or transformation, and those with form.

The formless realms, up to and including those who are neither with perception nor without perception—as clarified in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*—these twelve categories are all comprised within the realm of sentient beings.
However, once one realizes the four fruits of the path and transcends the three realms, one is no longer encompassed by these twelve classes.
Question: Both Zen meditation and the recitation of the Buddha’s name are equally intended for resolving the problem of birth and death. Our only concern is the nature of the mind.

It has not yet been clarified. If the nature of the mind were truly clarified, then what would not be the Pure Land? The three realms are fundamentally empty; how could there be anything that emerges from them?
The twelve categories of beings are not real; how could there be any identity among them? Even a Buddha cannot be apprehended, let alone sentient beings. [Question: Answer.
"What you have said is all name without substance; you merely seek momentary pleasure in debate, yet you understand nothing of profit or harm.

Let me question you: Have you realized the four fruits [of the śramaṇa]? He replied, 'Not yet. [The Master] said, 'Since you have not realized the four fruits, you are but an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
Upon the exhaustion of this life, you will certainly undergo future existence (punarbhava). If you undergo future existence, it will not be..."
Humans and devas are within the three miserable realms; they ultimately do not transcend the twelve categories of beings.

You are still unable to transcend the realm of desire, let alone the realm of form and the formless realm. You are still unable to transcend the three miserable realms, let alone transcend the Buddha’s inquiry.
Question: When a Śrāvaka realizes the four fruits of the path, their physical body still remains; is this not, therefore, included among the twelve categories of sentient beings? Answer:

Although the bodies of Śrāvakas who have realized the four fruits have not yet perished, they will perish before long. Once they have perished, they receive the Dharma-nature body (dharmatā-kāya) and dwell in the Land of Expedient Means (upāya-bhūmi), beyond the triple world (tridhātu).
They are like guests staying at an inn who do not remain for long but soon depart; as for their family members, [they likewise do not stay].
One must not regard them as mere members of a household. It is likewise with the śrāvakas who temporarily dwell within the triple world.
When the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas occasionally transform and deliver sentient beings by manifesting in the world, they must invariably rely upon parents and the womb.

Is it not also the case that they are born from a womb? To what category should they then be assigned? Answer: When the Buddhas deliver sentient beings, they manifest the appearance of a womb, a mother, and a father.

Since these are described as "manifestations," although they exist, they are not real. How could one then definitively categorize sentient beings and subsume them within the twelve classes of existence?
Furthermore, the two lands of the Quiescent Light and the True Reward are the original abodes of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This is merely a temporary manifestation. [Objection: If that is so, why do the sutras and treatises collectively refer to the ten dharma realms as "sentient beings" (*sattva*)?
[Response: This is a general discussion; for even those of the Three Vehicles who have emerged from the three realms still possess the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*).

The Buddha also possesses the five aggregates (*skandhas*) that are eternally abiding; thus, he receives that name. Now, however, we set aside the general [principle] to follow the specific, discussing only the death of individual subjects rather than transformation or eternal abiding.
Therefore, one cannot use that [case of the Buddha] to challenge this question.
Even though there is birth by transformation (*upapāduka*) in the Western Pure Land, is it not nonetheless subsumed within the twelve categories of beings? Answer: Although the Pure Land...

There are those born by transformation (*upapāduka*). However, their bodies are not composed of discrete parts; being purely and entirely transformation-born, they do not belong to the twelve classes [of beings].

(In this context, "part" refers to a limit and "segment" refers to a physical form. Because the lifespan in that land is immeasurable, there are no limits; because their physical forms transform without fixed direction and are neither existent nor non-existent, they lack physical segments.

Furthermore, once one is born in that land, one immediately enters the stream of the sages and proceeds directly to Buddhahood without ever again receiving a body. How, then, could such beings be designated as belonging to the twelve classes?

[The interlocutor] says: "It is somewhat like this. I ask those who have attained realization through the Chan school: once they have thoroughly penetrated the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), they neither exit nor enter the triple world (*tridhātu*);

they neither abandon nor accept the twelve classes of beings (*dvādaśa-vidha-sattva*). Dwelling wherever conditions lead them as a skillful means (*upāya*) to save sentient beings—what is there that is not permissible?

[The respondent] answers: "Although a realized person possesses such an insight, they have not yet severed their afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma (*karma*). If they were to be born within the three..."
The realms. As soon as one enters the womb, one is immediately separated from the previous life; what was previously realized is quickly forgotten.
The lifelong effort is lost in a single morning—is this not to be lamented? Furthermore, there is karma that drags one into other species;
how then could you maintain self-mastery and avoid being obstructed by evil retribution? If you are born in those lands, [you will be] personally...
Draw near to the Teacher. Once you have entered the ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*), you shall immediately ascend to the stage of Buddhahood.

When compared to this, consider who gains and who loses: those who drift and sink within the three realms (*tridhātu*) and pass through the cycle of birth in various wombs. You should reflect upon this for yourself. Therefore, know that it is better not to awaken at all than to awaken and yet fail to seek rebirth in the Western Land;
once awakened, one’s efforts must become even more urgent. It is like a person who has found a treasure: they must find a good place to bury it before they can truly possess it.
If one does not utilize it, it will ultimately be lost. Awakening and rebirth in the Pure Land are likewise.

You should know that for those wishing to transcend birth and death, there is no way superior to the single gate of the Pure Land; if one were able to achieve liberation while remaining in this world, such a thing would be impossible.
I pray that you refrain from contentious speech and instead reflect upon this with a tranquil mind.
Now, the mutual opposition between these two individuals is no different from the water in two gourds; yet they do not know to discard one and adopt the other—how grave this is!
(Note: according to the subsequent text, the phrase "there is surely delusion" [其惑也] should be supplied here.)
This concludes the preceding text to clarify the principles of rejection and acceptance.
Indeed, in this age of the Dharma’s semblance, it is not only religious practitioners whose fundamental tenets conflict like water from two different gourds;

even those who follow the same Dharma gate and study under the same teacher may possess differing insights, and such cases are numerous. This is because right view is difficult to encounter, while heterodox followers are easily found.
It has been a long time since we first met. Now, as we discuss what to adopt and what to reject, one ought to understand the benefits and harms.
As stated above, the consequences of belief and slander, of gain and loss, are perfectly clear. What wise person would not know how to choose between them? Alas!
Nowadays, there is no one who does not seek profit, yet they constantly suffer loss; there is no one who does not avoid harm, yet they constantly encounter it. Why is this so?
Generally speaking, this is because the mind is not empty, conduct is not sincere, and insight is not upright.
Therefore, those who cultivate the mind must strive to empty their minds, make their conduct sincere, and rectify their insight.

Taking the sacred teachings as a clear mirror and teachers and friends as a whip, they should remain vigilant and exert themselves with trembling awe from beginning to end; in this way, they may hope to avoid great harm.
Otherwise, one suffers harm for a lifetime, remaining complacent and unaware. Even when approaching death, one still fails to awaken;
thus, an entire life is spent in vain, leaving behind regrets that endure for a thousand ages. Such cases are numerous, all resulting from a failure to discern what to reject and what to adopt.
"How extreme! These are words of reproach, stating that wisdom is not equal to the water in a gourd floating on the sea. How deeply one may sigh!
[This concludes] the discourse of the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea."
